summary: Multicast VPNs can use PIM as the control protocol between provider edge routers, and UDP-based S-PMSI Join messages to bind customer multicast flows to provider tunnels. This RFC extends those options so they work for IPv6 as well.

plainLanguage.summary: Some mailing methods were written only for old-style addresses. This extends them so they work with the new, longer addresses too.

questions: what is a type 4 s-pmsi join
how does ipv6 multicast work over an ipv4 mvpn
subtitle: Lets IPv6 customer multicast ride across a provider network that builds its tunnels with IPv4 PIM.

tldr.problem: RFC 6513 describes multicast VPNs using PIM between provider edge routers and S-PMSI Join messages, but it does not cover customers who use IPv6 while the provider tunnels are built over IPv4.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a Type 4 S-PMSI Join that carries IPv6 customer source and group addresses plus an IPv4 tunnel group, and says how IPv6 PIM messages are addressed when they ride in GRE over IPv4.
tldr.outcome: Customers with IPv6 multicast flows can use the PIM and S-PMSI Join options of RFC 6513 over an IPv4 provider core. The RFC also allows several S-PMSI Joins in one UDP datagram.

today: RFC 6516 is a Proposed Standard from February 2012. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 6513.

sections.title: The Gap in the MVPN Specification
sections.content:
The Multicast VPN (MVPN) specification, RFC 6513, defines a PMSI (Provider Multicast Service Interface) and says how it can be built from tunnels across a service provider network, called P-tunnels. It also describes using PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast, RFC 4601) as the control protocol between Provider Edge (PE) routers. In that mode, PIM messages carrying customer multicast routing information travel through a P-tunnel from one PE to the others in the same MVPN.

RFC 6513 does not cover a customer that uses IPv6 while the provider builds its P-tunnels with PIM over an IPv4 infrastructure. It also defines optional S-PMSI Join messages, which bind particular customer multicast flows to particular P-tunnels, but only for IPv4 customer flows. This RFC fills both gaps and adds a rule for packing several S-PMSI Joins into one UDP datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook only explained how to deliver mail with old-style addresses. This new note adds the missing rules for the new-style addresses.

sections.title: Terms Borrowed from RFC 6513
sections.content:
The RFC reuses the vocabulary of RFC 6513: C-source, C-group, C-flow, P-group and (C-S,C-G). The C-prefixed terms describe the customer's multicast traffic: the source, the group address and the flow made of the two. The P-group is the address that identifies the provider's tunnel.

An existing Type 1 S-PMSI Join can assign a customer IPv4 (C-S,C-G) flow to a P-tunnel created by PIM over IPv4. Packets on such a tunnel are encapsulated in GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) within IPv4, as RFC 6513 specifies in its Section 12. The new message in this RFC keeps that same GRE/IPv4 tunnel and changes only the customer side.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer has a name for the thing being sent and the provider has a name for the truck carrying it. This RFC just reuses those names.

sections.title: The Type 4 S-PMSI Join
sections.content:
S-PMSI Join messages begin with a type field, and RFC 6513 defines only Type 1. This RFC defines Type 4, which assigns a customer IPv6 (C-S,C-G) flow to a P-tunnel created by PIM over IPv4. Data and control packets on the tunnel use GRE/IPv4 encapsulation.

  • Type (8 bits): 4.
  • Length (16 bits): 40, the length in octets of the whole message.
  • Reserved (8 bits): SHOULD be zero when sent and MUST be ignored when received.
  • C-source (128 bits): the IPv6 address of the traffic source in the VPN.
  • C-group (128 bits): the IPv6 group address of the multicast traffic.
  • P-group (32 bits): the IPv4 group address identifying the P-tunnel. Data packets on that tunnel carry this address as the destination of the outer IPv4 GRE header.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a short note that says: this stream from this sender to this group should travel on that truck. The sender and group use long addresses, and the truck uses a short one.

sections.title: UDP Encapsulation and IPv6 PIM Over IPv4
sections.content:
All S-PMSI Joins travel in UDP datagrams. A Type 4 S-PMSI Join MUST be sent in an IPv6 UDP datagram. The IPv6 source address of that datagram SHOULD be the IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (RFC 4291) that matches the IPv4 address the originating PE uses as its source in the PIM instance that creates the P-tunnel.

A single UDP datagram MAY carry several S-PMSI Joins, as many as fit entirely inside it. They MUST all be of the same type. The end of the last Join, found using the Join length field, MUST coincide with the end of the datagram given by the UDP length field. A router that receives such a datagram MUST process every Join in it.

When a customer runs PIM over IPv6 and the provider uses an IPv4-based control protocol for its P-tunnels, the PE routers must originate IPv6 PIM control messages. Their IPv6 source address SHOULD be the same kind of IPv4-mapped address. If the destination is the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group, the IPv6 form ff02::d is used. These messages are not sent natively across the provider network but are encapsulated in GRE/IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes go inside envelopes, and one envelope can hold several notes of the same kind. The sender's return address is made from its old-style address so replies know where to go.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 6513 created an IANA registry called the S-PMSI Join Message Type Field. This document registers a new value there: 4, described as GRE S-PMSI for IPv6 traffic (unaggregated).

The security section is one sentence: there are no additional security considerations beyond those of RFC 6513.
sections.plainLanguage: The new note type gets its own number in the official list. Nothing new needs guarding beyond what the old rules already cover.
